en: Speaking with sincerity and straightforwardness, with sincere mind and right faith—sincere mind and right faith—the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness."
Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Faith is like the water-clearing jewel,
for it can purify turbid water."
Thus we know that when the myriad virtues arise, faith serves as their precursor.
Therefore, Buddhist sūtras begin with "Thus have I heard," which is precisely what gives rise to faith.
Someone asked:
"What difference is there between the faith of the Patriarchal Gate and the faith of the Teaching Gate?
He replied: "There are many points of difference."
The teachings cause humans and devas to believe in cause and effect.
Those who cherish the joy of merit and happiness believe that the ten wholesome actions are the sublime cause.
Humans and devas constitute the fruit of pleasure.
For those who find joy in emptiness and stillness,
they believe that the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing constitute the true cause.
The noble fruits consist of the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path. Those who aspire to the fruit of Buddhahood believe that the three incalculable eons and the six perfections constitute the great causes.
Bodhi and Nirvana constitute the true fruit;
the authentic faith of the Patriarchal Gate is not like that of the former [teachings].
One does not believe in any causes and effects of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Simply believe that you are originally a Buddha.
The true, natural nature is fully possessed by every person;
the wondrous essence of nirvana is perfectly realized by each and every one.
There is no need to seek it from others; it has been fully prepared within oneself from the beginning.
The Third Patriarch said:
"Perfectly identical to the great void, without deficiency and without excess."
This is truly because their choosing and rejecting are not as they should be.
Master Zhigong said:
"Within the body with form is the body without form."
On the road of ignorance there is no road of non-arising. Yongjia said:
"The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature."
The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body;
thus, one knows that sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas.
Having given rise to right faith, one must further cultivate understanding.
Yongming said:
"To believe without understanding increases ignorance;
to understand without believing increases false views."
It is known that by combining the characteristics of faith and understanding, one may enter the Path swiftly.
Someone asked:
"If one has merely first given rise to the mind of faith but has not yet entered the Path, is there still any benefit?"
The *Awakening of Faith* says:
"If a person, having heard this Dharma, does not give rise to timidity or weakness,
one should know that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas."
They will certainly receive the prediction of enlightenment from all the Buddhas.
Suppose there were someone who could transform all the sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm, causing them to practice the ten virtuous deeds.
It is not equal to someone who, for even a single moment of thought, correctly contemplates this Dharma;
the merit of the former cannot be compared to it.
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
Even those who give rise to pure faith for but a single moment—
the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees them;
all such sentient beings shall obtain immeasurable merit and virtue.
Thus we know that if one wishes to travel a thousand li, the first step must be correct.
If the first step is wrong, the entire thousand li will be wrong.
To enter the land of non-action (*asamskṛta*), initial faith must be correct.
Once initial faith is lost, all myriad virtues recede together;
thus the Patriarch said:
"A difference of a hair's breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth."
This is the principle.
An alternative name for the true mind is, as some say,
"having already given rise to right faith."
It was not yet known what was called the "true mind. [The Master] said:
"That which is free from delusion is called 'true';
its numinous reflection is called 'mind'."
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* elucidates this mind.
Someone may ask:
"Is it merely that the 'true mind' has another distinct name?"
It is said that the names established by the ancestral teachings of Buddhism differ.
For instance, in Buddhism, the Bodhisattva precepts are called the "Mind-Ground" (cittabhūmi),
because they give rise to all manner of goodness.
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras refer to it as bodhi (awakening),
because its essence is identical to awakening.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra establishes it as the dharmadhātu (dharma-realm).
Because they are mutually interpenetrating and harmoniously integrated,
the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is titled "The Tathāgata.
Because he comes from nowhere, it is so named.
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras are called "Nirvāṇa" because they are the destination to which all sages return;
the Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra is titled "Tathatā."
Because it is truly eternal and unchanging,
the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* refers to it as the Dharmakāya;
because it is that upon which the Sambhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya rely.
In the *Awakening of Faith*, it is called True Suchness (*tathatā*) because it is neither born nor extinguished;
in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is referred to as Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Because it is the essential substance of the three bodies,
it is called "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*) within the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*;
because it flows forth from it as merit and virtue.
The Śrīmālā-sūtra is titled "Tathāgatagarbha" because it conceals,
encompasses, and contains [the Buddha-nature];
the definitive sūtra is named "Perfect Enlightenment" (Yuanjue).
Because it destroys darkness and shines alone, Master Shou’s *Vow of Mind-Only* states:
"A single Dharma has a thousand names; these titles are established in response to conditions."
The details are contained in the various sutras and cannot be cited in full.
Someone may say:
"I already know the Buddhist teachings."
"What is the nature of the Patriarchal Teaching?
He replied, "Under the gate of the Patriarchs, names and words are cut off.
Since no name can be established, how could there be many more names?"
The names by which one is addressed vary according to the capacities of those who encounter them;
at times one is called "Self," because it is the fundamental nature of sentient beings.
At times it is called the "True Eye," for it reflects all phenomenal appearances;
at times it is designated as the "Sublime Mind."
Because it is empty, luminous, and quiescently illuminating,
it is sometimes called the "Master.
Because it has borne the burden from time immemorial.
Sometimes it is called the bottomless bowl,
for it provides one's livelihood wherever one may be;
sometimes it is called the stringless lute.
Because its resonance emerges from the present moment,
it is sometimes called the "Inexhaustible Lamp";
because it illuminates and shatters deluded attachments.
At times it is called the rootless tree,
for its root and base are firm and stable;
at other times it is referred to as the "hair-cutting sword."
Because the sensory faculties are severed,
it is sometimes called the Unconditioned Realm;
because the seas are tranquil and the rivers are clear.
At times it is called the "Jewel of the Muni," because it benefits and relieves the poor;
at other times it is named the "Latchless Lock."
Because the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are closed,

it is designated by various alternative names such as the "mud ox," the "wooden horse," the "source of the mind" (*citta-srota*), the "mind-seal" (*citta-mudrā*), the "mirror of the mind" (*citta-ādarśa*), the "moon of the mind" (*citta-candra*),
and the "jewel of the mind" (*citta-maṇi*). These diverse names cannot be recorded in their entirety.
If one realizes the true mind, all names and designations will be fully understood;
if one is oblivious to this true mind, all names and designations will remain obstructed.
Therefore, one must be most diligent and meticulous regarding the true mind.
The Sublime Essence of the True Mind. Regarding the "Sublime Essence of the True Mind," some may ask:
"We already know the name of the True Mind;
what is its essence like?"
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra of the Emitted Light* states:
"Prajñā has no characteristics of existence and no characteristics of arising or ceasing.
The *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:
As for the self-substance of suchness,
it neither increases nor decreases across all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.
It is neither born in the past nor extinguished in the future;
it is ultimately eternal and constant.
From the very beginning, its nature has been spontaneously replete with all merits.
According to this sutra and its commentaries, the essential substance of the true mind transcends cause and effect and penetrates through all time, past and present;
it does not establish the distinction between ordinary beings and sages, nor does it admit any form of dualistic opposition.
Like the great void, it pervades all places;
its wondrous essence is concentrated and tranquil, transcending all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
it is neither born nor extinguished, neither existent nor non-existent.
Unmoving, unswaying, and profoundly still, eternally abiding—
this is called the original master;
he is named the person beyond the limit of Vairocana.
It is also called the self prior to the kalpa of emptiness;
it is a state of singular evenness, devoid of the slightest flaw or blemish.
All mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, forests, and the myriad phenomena of the phenomenal world are [this very state].
All phenomena, whether defiled or pure, emerge from within this.
Thus, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "Good son,"
The Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great *dhāraṇī* gateway called Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*),
from which flow forth all pure *tathatā*, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the *pāramitās*.
Regarding the instruction for bodhisattvas, Guifeng said:
"As for the mind..."
Vast, void, wondrous, and refined;
brilliant, radiant, numinous, and luminous.
Without going or coming, it darkly penetrates the three periods of time.
Neither internal nor external, it penetrates clearly throughout the ten directions;
being neither extinguished nor born,
how could it be harmed by the four mountains?
Being devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of characteristics, how could the five colors blind one?
Thus, the *Weixin jue* (Secret of Mind-Only) by Yongming says:
Now, this mind is where all wonders and the multitude of spirits universally converge;
it is the sovereign of the myriad dharmas.
The three vehicles and five natures all return to her in silent harmony;
she is the mother of a thousand sages,
uniquely honored and supreme, peerless and without equal.
This is truly the source of the Great Way and the essential core of the True Dharma.
To believe in it is for Bodhisattvas of the three periods to study together;
indeed, they study this very mind.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time have all realized this together;
it is precisely this mind that they have realized.
The entire Great Canon of teachings serves to explain and manifest it.
This is to reveal this mind.
That all sentient beings are deluded and confused is precisely because they are deluded regarding this mind.
All practitioners awaken; this is because they awaken to this mind.
All the patriarchs have transmitted it thus.
In short, this is the transmission of this mind.
When monks throughout the world go on pilgrimage and seek instruction,
they are seeking this very mind.
To realize this mind, every place is the Way and every thing is fully manifest;
to be deluded regarding this mind, one is inverted in every situation and maddened with folly in every thought.
This essence is the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by all sentient beings.
This is the very source from which all worlds arise; therefore,
the World-Honored One remained silent for a long time on Vulture Peak,
beneath the cliff of Subhūti.
Bodhidharma’s wall-contemplation at Shaoshi and the layman Vimalakīrti’s silence both serve to illuminate the wondrous essence of this mind.
Therefore, those who first enter the ancestral gate must first recognize the essence of this mind.
Regarding the wondrous function of the true mind, some say:
The wondrous essence is already known;
what, then, is called its wondrous function?
It is said that an ancient master remarked:
The wind stirs and the heart trembles like a tree;
clouds arise and the nature gives rise to dust.
If one understands the affairs of today, [one will see them as they truly are].
To obscure the person who is originally present is for the wondrous essence to give rise to its function;
the wondrous essence of the true mind is fundamentally unmoving.
Quiescent, true, and eternal.
Within the true essence, sublime function manifests before one;
thus, it does not hinder one from attaining the wondrous while following the flow.
Therefore, the Patriarch’s verse says:
"The mind turns following the myriad objects;
where it turns is truly profound."
Recognizing one's nature as it follows the stream,
there is neither joy nor sorrow; therefore,
at all times, one acts and exerts oneself through movement and function.
Walking east and going west, eating and dressing,
picking up the spoon and handling the chopsticks, looking left and right—
all these are the manifestation of the wondrous function of the true mind.
Ordinary people, deluded and inverted, understand only dressing when they are dressing;
they understand only eating when they are eating.
In all their activities, they merely follow along with appearances.
Therefore, one acts within daily life without awakening and perceives what is before one's eyes without knowing it.
This is the case for those whose nature is merely that of consciousness.
In all movement and activity, one has never been oblivious;
thus the Patriarch said:
"While in the womb, it is called spirit."
A person of renown in the world is observed by the eyes and heard by the ears.
One smells odors with the nose;
one converses with the mouth;
one grasps things with the hands.
Moving with the speed of a galloping horse,
it manifests everywhere, encompassing the entire Dharma-realm;
yet when withdrawn, it is contained within a single minute atom.
Those who know it call it Buddha-nature;
those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit.
This is why it is said: "Wu dances with his ritual tablet."
Shigong brandishes his bow;
Bimozha holds up his pitchfork;
Juzhi points upward with a finger.
From Xinzhou Dazi to Yunyan Shizi,
there were none who did not illuminate this great function.
If one is not deluded in daily activities, then naturally there will be no obstruction regardless of how one acts.
Regarding the identity or difference between the essence and function of the true mind, some say: [the following].
I do not yet understand whether the essence and function of the true mind are one or different.
He replied: "In terms of their phenomenal characteristics, they are not one;
in terms of their fundamental nature, they are not different."
Therefore, this essence and its function are neither identical nor different.
How is this known to be so?
Let us attempt to discuss it.
The wondrous essence is immovable, transcending all opposition and free from all characteristics;
its principle cannot be fathomed by anyone who has not realized its nature through direct realization.
Its wondrous function responds to conditions according to the myriad categories of beings;
it falsely establishes empty resemblances that appear to have form and shape.
Because it is defined by these aspects of having form and lacking form, it is not one.
Furthermore, function arises from essence without departing from it;
essence can give rise to function without departing from it.
Because they are inseparable according to this principle, they are not different.
Just as water takes moisture as its substance,
and because that substance is motionless,
waves take movement as their characteristic.
Because they arise due to the wind, the nature of water and the characteristics of its waves differ in their movement and stillness; thus, they are not one and the same.
Nevertheless, there is no water apart from the waves, and no waves apart from the water.
Since moisture is a single entity, it is not something separate.
By analogy, the identity or difference between essence and function can be understood.
Regarding the true mind in delusion, it is said that the true mind exists within delusion. Or, as it is said: [the true mind in delusion].
The essence of the true mind is possessed by everyone;
why then is there a difference between the sage and the ordinary person?
It is said: the true mind is fundamentally the same for both sages and ordinary persons.
Ordinary beings, with their deluded minds,
recognize external objects and lose their own pure nature,
being obstructed by them; therefore, the true mind cannot manifest before them.
It is simply like tree shadows in the dark or a spring flowing beneath the earth;
they exist, yet one does not recognize them.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel that reflects the five colors, each appearing according to its direction.
Foolish people see those five colors as being truly present in the maṇi.
"Good son, the pure nature of perfect enlightenment manifests within body and mind, responding to each according to its kind.
Those who are deluded claim that this pure, perfect enlightenment truly possesses such a body and mind."
The intrinsic nature is likewise so.
The *Zhao lun* says:
"Within the realm of heaven and earth, and between the boundaries of the universe..."
"Within it there is a precious jewel secretly hidden in the mountain of form;
this refers to the true mind remaining within the bonds of existence.
Furthermore, Ci'en says:
The Dharma-body is originally present and common to all Buddhas;
yet ordinary beings, due to being shrouded by delusion, do not realize its existence.
Enveloped by afflictions, it is given the name "Tathāgatagarbha."
Lord Pei said:
"One who is in perfect enlightenment all day long yet never perceives it as such is an ordinary person.
Thus we know that although the true mind exists amidst the toils of worldly existence, it is not defiled by those worldly toils."
It is like throwing white jade into mud; its color does not change.
Regarding the phrase "the true mind ceases delusion," some say:
"If the true mind exists within delusion, then one is an ordinary person."
How can one attain sainthood by means of delusion?
It is said that the ancients remarked:
"When the deluded mind has no place to abide, that is bodhi."
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are fundamentally equal.
As the Sūtra says:
"When the illusory body of those sentient beings ceases, their illusory mind also ceases."
Because illusory mind ceases, illusory objects also cease.
Because illusory objects cease, the cessation of illusion also ceases.
Because the cessation of illusion ceases, that which is not illusory does not cease.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, the clarity appears.
Yongjia also said:
"The mind is the root; dharmas are the dust."
The two [aspects] are like blemishes upon a mirror;
when the stains of these blemishes are exhausted, the light finally appears.
When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, the nature is itself the truth.
This is the emergence of the true from the delusory. Someone may say:
"The Master Zhuang said that the mind is as hot as a blazing fire."
Its cold freezes the ice;
its swiftness, in the space of a single bow or a nod,
reaches twice beyond the four seas.
That which abides in depth and stillness,
and moves with suspension and heavenly spontaneity—
is it not the human mind?
This was how Zhuangzi previously stated that the mind of an ordinary person cannot be tamed or subdued.
I do not yet know by what method the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) treats this deluded mind.
He replied: "One treats the deluded mind with the method of no-mind."
Someone said:
"If a person has no mind, they would be the same as grass and trees.
I pray that you will provide a skillful means for this teaching of 'no-mind'."
It is said: "Now, when we speak of 'no-mind,' it does not mean that the substance of mind is absent and thus called no-mind.
Rather, it is called no-mind because there are no objects within the mind."
It is like speaking of an "empty bottle.
A bottle that contains no objects within it is called an "empty bottle";
it is not that the substance of the bottle itself is non-existent that it is called an "empty bottle."
Therefore, the Patriarch said:
"You need only have no affairs within the mind and no mind toward affairs;
then naturally it will be empty yet spiritual, still yet wondrous."
This is the essential purport of this mind.
Based on this, it follows that while there is no deluded mind, it does not mean that the wondrous functioning of the true mind is absent.
Thus have the various masters of old explained it.
The various types of practice for "effortless cultivation" (wuxin gongfu) differ from one another.
Here, I shall briefly clarify ten general categories according to their broad principles.
The first is called "alert observation" (jiucha).
This means that when practicing, one should normally sever all thoughts and maintain a defensive vigilance against their arising;
as soon as a single thought is born, it must be immediately recognized and shattered through awareness.
When deluded thoughts are shattered by awakening, subsequent thoughts do not arise;
even this awakening-intelligence need not be employed.
When both delusion and awakening are forgotten, it is called "no-mind."
Therefore, the Patriarch said:
"I do not fear the arising of thoughts; I only fear that awakening is late.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"Do not seek the Truth; you need only cease [false] views.
This is the practice for ceasing delusion.
Second is "resting."
This means that when practicing, do not think of good and do not think of evil;
as soon as a thought arises, let it rest; as soon as you encounter conditions, let them cease.
An ancient said:
"A single length of white silk goes;
it goes off cold and still."
The incense burner has departed from the ancient temple;
it must reach the point where all finicky attachments are severed and all dualistic discrimination is abandoned.
Only when one is as if dazed or like a pillar will there be a slight degree of resonance with reality.
This is the practice of resting the deluded mind.
Third is "merging the mind with its object," which refers to the time when one is engaged in the practice.
When all deluded thoughts have ceased together,
one disregards external objects and simply allows the mind to rest within itself.
Once the deluded mind has ceased, what harm can there be in the presence of objects?
This is precisely the ancient teaching of "seizing the person but not seizing the environment.
Thus, there is a saying:
"In this place there are fragrant herbs; throughout the city, there is no old friend."
Furthermore, Pang Gong said:
"If one simply remains without a mind toward the myriad things,
what harm is there in the myriad things constantly surrounding one?"
This is the practice of extinguishing the mind while maintaining the object to still delusive thoughts.
Fourth is extinguishing the object while maintaining the mind;
this refers to when one is performing the practice.
One should contemplate all internal and external objects as entirely empty and quiescent,
leaving only the single mind standing solitary and independent.
Thus, an ancient said:
It does not consort with the myriad dharmas,
nor does it confront the various sensory objects.
If the mind clings to objects, that mind is itself delusion.
Now that objects no longer exist, what delusion could there be?
Thus, the true mind shines alone, unimpeded by the Way;
this is what the ancients meant by "taking away the object, not taking away the person."
Thus there is a saying:
"The flowers in the upper garden have already withered, yet carriages and horses still throng there.
And it is also said:
"Where are the three thousand swordsmen now?
Zhuang Zhou alone plans for peace and stability.
This refers to the practice of dissolving the sensory realm, preserving the mind, and quelling delusions.
Fifth, the stilling of both mind and objects:
this means that when practicing,
one first empties and quiets external objects.
Next, one extinguishes the internal mind.
Once both the external environment and the internal mind are tranquil,
how could delusion ultimately exist?
Therefore, Guankui said:
"The ten directions have no walls, and the four sides have no gates;
it is pure and naked, stark and clear."
This is precisely the patriarchal teaching of the "simultaneous withdrawal of both person and environment.
Thus, there is a saying:
"The clouds disperse and the waters flow away; the heavens and earth are silent and empty."
It is further said:
"When neither person nor ox is seen, this is precisely the time when the moon is bright.
This refers to the practice of quelling the mind and quelling objects, thereby bringing delusive thoughts to rest.
Sixth, the preservation of both object and mind:
this means that when practicing,
the mind abides in its own state and the object abides in its own state.
At times, when mind and object face one another,
the mind does not grasp the object and the object does not confront the mind; each remains without reaching the other.
Delusive thoughts do not arise spontaneously,
for there is no obstruction regarding the Way.
As the Sūtra says:
"This Dharma abides in its fixed position; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.
This is precisely the patriarchal teaching wherein both person and environment are not usurped.
Thus, there is a saying:
"A single moon rises over the sea; how many families ascend their towers?
It is also said:
"Myriad mountain flowers in their thousands, yet the traveler knows not of returning."
This is the practice of maintaining both the object and the mind to extinguish delusion.
Seventh, the "entirety of the internal and external" refers to the time when one is performing the practice.
Within the mountains, rivers, great earth, sun, moon, and stars— the internal body and the external vessel—
all phenomena are identical in essence with the true mind;
they are profoundly still, empty, and luminous.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of difference.
The great trichiliocosm and all its realms are forged into a single piece.
Where else could a deluded mind possibly come from?
Therefore, Master Zhao said:
"Heaven and earth share the same root as I;
the myriad things share the same substance as I."
This is the practice of completely extinguishing delusions throughout both the internal and external spheres.
Eighth, the complete application of both the internal and external:
this refers to the time when one is practicing the功夫 (kungfu/practice).
One should contemplate all internal and external phenomena— including body, mind, and the physical world—
as well as all movements, activities, and functions,
as being entirely the wondrous functioning of the true mind.
As soon as any thought arises, it is the manifestation of wondrous function.
Since everything is this wondrous function,
where can a deluded mind possibly find a place to settle?
Thus Yongjia said:
"The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature;
the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body."
Master Zhì’s Song of the Twelve Hours says:
"At dawn, at the hour of Yín,
within the frantic mechanism, the person of the Way is hidden."
Whether sitting or reclining, one does not know that this is fundamentally the Way;
thus one merely wanders in haste, undergoing suffering and toil.
This is the complete application of the practice of quelling delusions both internally and externally.
The ninth is both essence and function.
This means that when one exerts effort in practice,
although one is in profound accord with the true essence— a single flavor of emptiness and stillness— this is so.
Within that [insight], the hidden spiritual luminosity is the essence as function;
within that spiritual luminosity, the hidden emptiness and stillness is the function as essence.
Thus Yongjia said:
Vigilant stillness is not the delusion of vigilance;
stillness within vigilance is not the stillness of the indeterminate state.
Since the indeterminate state cannot be admitted within stillness, [it is not that].
Within this state of alert awareness, do not allow discursive thoughts to arise; how could any deluded mind possibly be produced?
This is the practice of extinguishing delusion by unifying essence and function.
Tenth is the penetration of essence and function.
This means that when practicing the work,
one does not differentiate between internal and external.
Nor does one distinguish between east, west, south,
and north; rather, the four quarters and eight directions are made into a single, perfectly round gate of great liberation.
Essence and function are inseparable, without the slightest leakage;
the entire body is forged into a single piece—
where, then, could delusion possibly arise?
An ancient said:
"The entire body is without seams or gaps; above and below, it is perfectly round.
This refers to the practice of penetrating through essence and function to extinguish delusion.
Of the ten methods for practicing cultivation mentioned above, it is not necessary to employ them all.
It suffices to achieve mastery in even one method;
then delusion will naturally cease and the true mind will manifest.
According to one's faculties and past habitual tendencies, one will immediately practice whatever dharma one has had a karmic affinity for.
This effort is an effort of non-effort;
it is not the power of a deliberate mind.
Because this dharma-gate of resting the deluded mind is of the utmost importance, it is explained extensively;
there is no need for further textual elaboration.
Regarding the "four modes of conduct of the true mind," some say:

It was previously stated that one should practice calming the delusions; however, it is not yet clear whether this applies only to sitting meditation or also to walking, standing, and so forth. [The response is:
Most sūtras and śāstras speak primarily of practicing while sitting.
Because it is easily accomplished; furthermore,
it proceeds through the stages of practice and abiding,
gradually becoming fully matured over a long period.
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"If one practices *śamatha*,
one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright, and set the mind correctly."
Not relying on inhalation or exhalation;
not relying on form or color;
not relying on space.
Not relying on earth, water, fire, or wind,
and so forth, not relying on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing;
all perceptions and recollections are entirely eliminated.
One should also eliminate conceptualization,
for all phenomena are originally without conceptualization;
in every thought-moment they do not arise, and in every thought-moment they do not cease.
Furthermore, one must not follow after external objects of thought with the mind and then attempt to remove that mind with the mind.
If the mind wanders and scatters, it should immediately be drawn back and established in right mindfulness.
As for this right mindfulness:
One should know that there is only mind and no external objects;
furthermore, this very mind lacks any intrinsic nature,
being ungraspable in every moment of thought.
Whether rising from his seat, going or coming, advancing or stopping, or performing any activity,
at all times he constantly maintains mindfulness of skillful means and observes accordingly;
through long practice and mastery, his mind attains stability.
Because the mind abides [in this state], it gradually becomes sharp and intense;
accordingly, one enters the samādhi of suchness (tathatā).
Afflictions are deeply suppressed, and faith increases.
One will swiftly attain non-retrogression;
however, those who harbor doubt and lack faith, who slander [the teaching], who possess heavy karmic obstructions,
or who are arrogant and indolent— such persons as these cannot enter.
Based on this, it applies to all four modes of conduct.
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:
"First, rely upon the Tathāgata’s practice of śamatha."
He steadfastly maintains the prohibitive precepts,
dwells at ease among his followers,
and sits in meditative seclusion within a quiet chamber.
This is the beginning of practice. Yongjia said:
"Walking is Chan; sitting is also Chan."
Whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, the body remains at ease;
according to this, it also applies to the four modes of conduct.
Generally speaking, as for the power of cultivation, even sitting cannot yet bring the mind to rest.
How much less could walking, standing, and so forth enable one to enter the Way?
If it is a person whose mastery of these functions is pure and mature,
they will not be startled even if a thousand sages arise.
Ten thousand kinds of demons and malevolent spirits will not dare to look back;
how much less could one fail to practice the Way while walking, standing, or sitting?
It is like a person who harbors a deep resentment toward another.
Even in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, eating, drinking,
and all daily activities, one cannot forget it at any time;
the desire to love others is likewise thus.
Furthermore, hatred and love are matters within the mind;
they may still be accommodated within the state of having a mind.
However, the practice of spiritual cultivation now is a matter of being without a mind.
Why, then, should one doubt that these four modes of conduct do not manifest constantly?
I fear only that you do not believe in them or do not practice them;
if you do so and have faith, you will certainly not lose the Middle Way within your dignified deportment.
Regarding the locus of the true mind: some say that when deluded thoughts cease, the true mind manifests.
If this is so, where does the essence and function of the true mind reside now?
It is said that the wondrous essence of the true mind pervades all places. Yongjia said:
"Without departing from this very spot, it is eternally serene."
If you seek it, you will know that it cannot be seen.
As the Sūtra says:
"Because its nature is like empty space."
Because it is eternally unmoving;
because there is no arising or ceasing within the Tathāgatagarbha.
Thus says the Great Dharma-Eye:
Everywhere is the path to Bodhi; at every turn is a grove of merit.
This is precisely where the essence resides.
The wondrous function of the true mind manifests in accordance with conditions as they arise.
It is like an echo responding to a sound.
Faldeng said: "From ancient times to the present, there has never been a lapse."
Clearly present before one's eyes:
a fragment of cloud rises in the late valley;
a solitary crane descends from the distant sky.
Therefore, Yuan Hua-yan of the Wei Prefecture said:
"The Buddha-dharma is present in the midst of daily activities;
it is present in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining."
In places where one drinks tea and eats rice,
in places where one speaks and exchanges greetings,
and in all actions and deeds where the mind is raised and thoughts are stirred.
Furthermore, it is not that they are separate;
thus we know that the essence pervades all places and is fully capable of giving rise to function.
However, because the presence or absence of causes and conditions is not fixed,
its wondrous function is likewise not fixed;
it is not that there is no wondrous function.

Those who cultivate the mind and wish to enter the ocean of non-action to deliver all beings from birth and death must not be deluded regarding the locus of the true mind’s essence and function. Regarding "the true mind transcends death," it is said:
"The true mind transcends death. Or it is said: [The true mind transcends death.]
I have heard that those who have realized their nature transcend birth and death;
yet, although the patriarchs of the past were all such persons who had realized their nature,
they all experienced both birth and death.
"Now we see in the world that those who practice the Way still undergo the affairs of birth and death.
How can you say they transcend birth and death?
He replied, "Birth and death are fundamentally non-existent; it is through false conceptualization that they are taken to exist."
It is like a person with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky;
or when a healthy person says there are no such flowers,
the one with the disease does not believe them.
If the eye ailment ceases of its own accord without the appearance of floating flowers, only then will one believe the flowers were non-existent;
yet even while the flowers have not ceased, those flowers are themselves empty.
It is merely that the sick person falsely clings to it as being flowers;
they do not exist as substantial entities.
It is like a person who falsely identifies birth and death as existing.
Or, if someone who is neither born nor dying is told,
"Fundamentally, there is no birth and death," that person may, in a single day, falsely cease [the notion of] birth and death, and birth and death will naturally be eliminated.
Only then do you know that birth and death are fundamentally non-existent;
even when birth and death have not yet ceased, they are not truly existent,
for one falsely recognizes them as being present.
The Sūtra says:
"Good son, all sentient beings,
from time immemorial, have undergone various kinds of inversions."
It is like a person who has lost their way and confuses the four directions;
they falsely take the four elements to be the characteristics of their own body,
and the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects to be the characteristics of their own mind.
It is like those with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky;
even as these various empty flowers vanish into space,
one cannot say that there is a fixed place where they are extinguished.
Why is this? Because there is no place of birth.
All sentient beings, within that which is unborn, falsely perceive arising and ceasing.

Therefore, it is called "revolving in birth and death. Based on this scriptural passage, one can know with certainty that the perfectly enlightened true mind is fundamentally free from birth and death;
now one knows there is no birth and death.
Yet, those who are unable to escape birth and death do so because their diligent effort has not reached its consummation.
Therefore, it is said in the teachings:
The woman Āmrapālī asked Mañjuśrī:
"If you clearly know that birth is the dharma of non-birth,
for what reason are you carried away by birth and death?"
Mañjuśrī said,
"Because his power was not yet sufficient.
Later, there was another who advanced to become the mountain master.
Xiu Shan’s Master asked:
"If you clearly know that birth is the dharma of non-birth,
why are you nonetheless carried away by birth and death?"
Xiu said: "A bamboo shoot will ultimately become a bamboo pole.
Now, can it be used as bamboo strips?"
Therefore, knowing that there is no birth-and-death is not as good as realizing that there is no birth-and-death;
realizing that there is no birth-and-death is not as good as conforming to the fact that there is no birth-and-death;
and conforming to the fact that there is no birth-and-death is not as good as functioning within the absence of birth-and-death.
People today do not even know that there is no birth-and-death;
how much less could they embody the absence of birth-and-death, accord with the absence of birth-and-death, or function within the absence of birth-and-death?
Therefore, those who cling to birth-and-death do not believe in the dharma of the absence of birth-and-death.
Is this not indeed appropriate?
Regarding "the true mind as the primary and the auxiliary":
some say that when delusions have ceased as previously described, the true mind manifests before one.
Furthermore, while delusion has not yet ceased,
one simply rests to cultivate the practice of "no-mind.
Are there any other methods that can serve as an antidote to these various delusions?
It is said that the primary and the auxiliary differ.
Taking the cessation of delusion through a mind of non-activity as the primary,
and the cultivation of various virtues as the auxiliary.
For example, it is like a bright mirror covered by dust;
although one may scrub and wipe it with the strength of one's hands,
its radiance will only appear when it is polished with a sublime medicinal ointment.
Dust and grime are the afflictions (*kleśa*);
manual labor is the merit of non-intentionality;
grinding medicine is the multitude of wholesome deeds (*kuśala*).
The mirror-light is the true mind.
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"Furthermore, regarding the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith..."
What kind of mind is generated?
Briefly, there are three types.
What are these three?
First is the straightforward mind,
because it maintains right mindfulness of the dharma of suchness.
Second is the profound mind.
Third is the mind of great compassion, because one desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings. This is because it gathers all virtuous practices.
Question: It was stated above that the dharma-realm has a single characteristic and the essence of the Buddha is non-dual.
For what reason, then, does one not simply contemplate True Suchness alone?
Furthermore, one must rely on seeking out various virtues through study.
The answer is:
It is like a great maṇi jewel whose essential nature is luminous and pure, yet which possesses the impurities of mineral dross.
Even if a person contemplates the nature of a jewel,
it will never become pure unless it is polished and refined through various skillful means;
for the defilements are immeasurable and pervade all phenomena.
One cultivates all wholesome practices.
Thus, although the essential nature of the dharma-body of suchness is empty and pure,
it is nevertheless defiled by immeasurable afflictions and impurities.
Even if a person contemplates True Suchness (tathatā),
they will not attain purity without the various types of cultivation through skillful means;
for defilements are immeasurable and pervade all phenomena.
One should cultivate all wholesome practices as an antidote;
for if a person practices all wholesome dharmas,
they will naturally accord with and conform to the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā).
According to this discussion,
resting the deluded mind is the primary practice,
while cultivating various wholesome dharmas serves as an auxiliary support.
If, when cultivating goodness, one is associated with a state of non-mind and does not grasp at cause and effect,
yet if one were to grasp at cause and effect, one would fall into the retributions of ordinary beings among humans and devas;
it would be difficult to realize True Suchness and one would not escape birth and death.
If one accords with the mindless state, this is the essential method for realizing *tathatā* (suchness) and escaping birth and death;
it simultaneously yields vast merit and virtue.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
Subhūti, the merit of a bodhisattva who practices giving without dwelling upon signs is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Now, we see among people of this world those who study and practice.
As soon as one knows that there is this original Buddha-nature,
one then relies on this innate spontaneity and fails to cultivate various virtues; thus, not only does one fail to realize the true mind,
but one even turns it into indolence.
One cannot even escape the evil realms,
let alone transcend birth and death;
this view is a great error.
Regarding the merit of the true mind: some say that if there is a mind that cultivates causes, there is the merit of being free from doubt;
but if there is no mind cultivating causes, from where does merit arise?
It is said: "Cultivating causes with a mind results in conditioned fruits;
acting without a mind as the cause reveals the merits of one's nature.
These various merits are inherently and spontaneously possessed from the very beginning."
Delusion concealed it so that it was not manifest;
now that delusion has been removed, its merit appears before one.
Thus Yongjia said:
The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within the essence;
the eight liberations and six supernormal powers are the mind-ground seal.
These are the inherent qualities and virtues spontaneously possessed within that essence.
An ancient verse says:
"If a person sits in meditation for even a single moment, it is superior to constructing stūpas made of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Those stūpas will ultimately turn to dust."
"One thought of pure mind achieves perfect enlightenment.
Thus we know that the merit of no-mind is greater than that of having a mind.
The Venerable Shuilao of Hongzhou went to visit Mazu and asked:
"What is the meaning of that which has come from the West?"— upon being kicked by Mazu,
he was suddenly awakened and clapped his hands in realization.
He laughed loudly and said:
"How extraordinary! How extraordinary!
Within these hundreds of thousands of samādhis lie immeasurable subtle meanings."
"Upon a single hair-tip, one immediately realizes the root source.
Thereupon, he paid homage and withdrew.
According to this, merit does not come from without.
"It is inherently complete.
The Fourth Patriarch said to Chan Master Lanrong:
"The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all converge within the single square inch of the mind."
The merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all within the source of the mind.
All gates of precept, concentration, and wisdom, as well as supernatural powers and transformations,
are entirely and spontaneously complete, never departing from your own mind— according to the words of the Patriarchs.
The merit of the mindless state is exceedingly great;
it is only those who value the characteristics of conditioned phenomena who fail to give rise to faith in the merit of the mindless state.
Verifying the Efficacy of the True Mind. Someone asked:
"When the true mind manifests before one, how does one know that this true mind has matured and is unimpeded?
He replied: "When a student of the Way has attained the manifestation of the true mind,"
However, because habitual tendencies have not yet been eliminated,
if one encounters a familiar object, there are times when mindfulness is lost;
it is like a trained ox that, even though disciplined, still follows along when pulled by the lead rope.
One still dares not let go of the reins;
one must wait until the mind is harmonized and the pace is steady, so that upon entering the crops, they do no harm to the seedlings—
only then does one dare to release the hand.
Having reached this stage, there is no need for the cowherd’s whip or rope;
naturally, the crops will not be harmed.
This is like a practitioner who, having attained the true mind, [no longer requires external discipline].
First, apply yourself to practice and preserve [your nature];
only when you possess great power of application can you benefit sentient beings.
When you verify this true mind, [you will realize its nature].
First, take those objects you have cherished throughout your life and repeatedly bring them to mind as if they were right before you. If, as before,
feelings of aversion or attachment arise toward them, [proceed accordingly].
This indicates that the mind of the Way has not yet matured;
if one does not give rise to feelings of aversion or attachment,
then the mind of the Way has matured.
Although it has matured in this way,
it is still not yet the case that aversion and attachment arise spontaneously;
therefore, examine the mind once more.
When encountering objects of aversion or attraction,
if one specifically gives rise to aversive or attractive thoughts to grasp those objects of aversion and attraction,
the mind is obstructed; if such thoughts do not arise, the mind is unobstructed.
It is like a white ox in an open field that does not damage the crops.
In antiquity, there were those who reviled the Buddhas and scolded the Patriarchs;
this was because their minds were in accord with this [true] mind. Now, we see that as soon as one enters the Gate of the School, [this realization occurs].
To study the disparagement of Buddhas and the reviling of patriarchs before one even knows the distance to the Way is to be far too presumptuous.
"The True Mind has no cognition; the True Mind has no cognition. Someone asks:
"When the True Mind and the deluded mind encounter an object, how does one distinguish between the true and the deluded?"
It is said that the deluded mind cognizes objects;
in response to favorable or adverse objects, it gives rise to greed and hatred,
and toward neutral objects, it gives rise to ignorance.
Since greed, hatred, and ignorance— the three poisons— arise toward objects,
it is clearly evident that this is the deluded mind.
As the Patriarch said:
The conflict between the contrary and the compliant is the disease of the mind;
thus we know that that which faces the acceptable and the unacceptable is the deluded mind.
If it were the true mind, it would be without knowing yet all-knowing.
Because it is equanimous and universally illuminating, it differs from grasses and trees;
because it gives rise to neither hatred nor attachment, it differs from the deluded mind.
Thus, in the presence of objects, it is empty and luminous, neither hating nor loving.
That which knows while being without knowledge is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*).
The *Treatise by Zhaolun* states:
"As for the Sage's mind..."
Subtle and signless, it cannot be regarded as existent;
yet its functioning is ever more diligent, so it cannot be regarded as non-existent.
Even to the point that because it is not existent, one knows while being without knowing.
It is not that there is no knowledge because of the absence [of a knowing subject], but rather that through non-knowing one knows. Thus, non-knowing is itself knowing;
there is nothing by which it can be said to differ from the mind of a sage.
Furthermore, the deluded mind clings to existence when it encounters existence and clings to non-existence when it encounters non-existence;
it constantly dwells within these two extremes and fails to know the Middle Way. Yongjia said:
To abandon deluded mind and grasp at ultimate truth—
this very mind of grasping and abandoning becomes artful hypocrisy.
Students of the Way who do not understand this employ it in their practice.
One deeply comes to recognize the thief as having been taken for a son.
If it were the true mind, it would abide in both existence and non-existence without falling into either;
for it constantly dwells in the Middle Way.
The Patriarch said:
"Do not pursue that which has conditions; do not dwell in the patience of emptiness.
With a single state of even-mindedness, all things are naturally extinguished."
The *Zhao lun* states:
"Therefore, the sage dwells in existence while not being existent; he abides in non-existence while not being non-existent."
Although they do not grasp at existence or non-existence,
they do not abandon existence or non-existence; therefore,
they blend their light with the defilements of worldly toil and circulate through the five realms of rebirth.
He departs in silence and arrives with quiet composure;
he is tranquil and non-active, yet there is nothing he does not do.
This describes the Sage extending his hand to benefit others.
He circulates through the five destinies to guide and transform sentient beings;
though he comes and goes, there is no characteristic of coming and going.
The deluded mind is not like this.
Therefore, the true mind and the deluded mind are not the same.
Furthermore, the true mind is the ordinary mind;
the deluded mind is the non-ordinary mind.
Someone asked:
"What is meant by 'ordinary mind'?
He replied: "Every person possesses a single point of numinous clarity."
Profoundly still like empty space, it pervades all places;
in relation to conventional phenomena, it is provisionally named "rational nature" (li-xing),
and in relation to deluded consciousness, it is metaphorically designated as the "true mind" (zhen-xin).
There is not the slightest bit of discrimination;
encountering conditions, one is never deluded.
There is not a single thought of grasping or rejecting.
Touching all things with universal pervasiveness,
it does not shift or change in accordance with the myriad objects of experience;
even if one follows the current, one attains the wondrous.
Without leaving its original place, it is profoundly still;
seek it and you know it, yet you do not see it—
this is the true mind.
Someone asked:
"What is meant by 'not the ordinary mind'? He replied:
"Objects of perception consist of both the sacred and the mundane."
Objects of experience are either defiled or pure;
objects of experience are either subject to cessation or eternal;
objects of experience consist of both principle and phenomena.
Objects have arising and ceasing;
objects have movement and stillness;
objects have going and coming.
Objects of experience may be beautiful or ugly;
objects of experience may be wholesome or unwholesome;
objects of experience may be cause or fruit.
Were one to discuss this in detail, there would be ten thousand variations and a thousand distinctions;
for now, however, we shall cite ten pairs, all of which are termed "extraordinary objects.
The mind arises in accordance with these extraordinary objects.
It does not cease within the ordinary realm;
rather, it is the mind that is not ordinary which faces the ordinary true mind before it.
Therefore, it is called the "not-ordinary deluded mind."
The true mind is inherently present;
it does not give rise to various distinctions according to ordinary circumstances,
and for this reason it is called the "ordinary true mind."
Someone asked:
"The true mind is ordinary and constant, devoid of any diverse causes.
Why then does the Buddha speak of cause and effect, and the retribution for good and evil?"
It is said: the deluded mind pursues various objects;
failing to understand these various objects, it subsequently gives rise to various states of mind.
The Buddha taught various dharmas of cause and effect to subdue and govern the various deluded minds; thus, cause and effect must be established.
If this true mind does not pursue various objects, [it remains as it is].
Because of this, various states of mind do not arise;
the Buddha then does not preach various dharmas.
How, then, could there be cause and effect?
Someone asked:
"Is it that the true mind is ordinarily unarisen?
He replied: "The true mind sometimes functions through application, but it does not arise by following after objects."
It is simply that their wondrous functioning and playful manifestation do not obscure the laws of cause and effect.
Regarding the phrase "where the true mind goes, there it goes," some say this refers to those who have not yet attained the true mind.
Due to delusion regarding the true mind, one creates the causes of good and evil.
Because of creating the cause of good, one is born within the good realms;
because of creating the cause of evil, one enters the evil realms.
That one undergoes birth according to karma is a principle beyond doubt. However,
for one who has realized the True Mind and whose deluded emotions have completely ceased, having attained realization of the True Mind where there are no causes of good or evil—
what reliance can that solitary spirit have after the body perishes?
It is said: "Do not say that those who have a support are superior to those who have no support.
Furthermore, do not equate those without support with the wayward sons who drift aimlessly in the human world."
"Like a solitary soul in the realm of hungry ghosts who has no master,
I specifically ask this question to seek a place of reliance.
Another said, "So it is."
It is said that this is not the case for one who has realized their nature.
Because all sentient beings are deluded regarding the awakened nature,
they forget their true feelings and thoughts, taking the formation of karmic bonds as their cause.
Born within the six realms of existence, one undergoes the retribution of good and evil.
For example, if karma of the celestial realm serves as the cause, one receives only the fruit of that celestial state;
apart from the specific place of rebirth to which one is joined, all other [fruits] cannot be experienced or utilized.
All realms of existence are likewise;
since they arise from karma,
one is born into a place of pleasure that accords with it.
The place of non-arising is not a state of bliss.
One takes the place of arising as one's own reliance,
while taking the place of non-arising as the reliance of others.
Therefore, where there is deluded sentiment, there is a deluded cause;
where there is a deluded cause, there is a deluded effect;
and where there is a deluded effect, there is a basis for reliance.
Where there is dependence, one distinguishes between self and other;
where one distinguishes between self and other, there is what is acceptable and what is unacceptable.
Now, having realized the true mind, one accords with the awakened nature that is free from arising and ceasing.
It gives rise to the wondrous function of non-arising and non-ceasing.
The wondrous essence is truly eternal and fundamentally without arising or ceasing;
the wondrous function follows conditions and appears to have arising and ceasing.
However, since function arises from essence and function is itself essence,
how could there be arising and ceasing?
One who realizes this attains the true essence.
What interference could there be between arising and ceasing?
It is like water, which takes moisture as its essence and waves as its function;
since the nature of moisture is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, [the waves do not arise or cease].
How could the moist nature within the waves arise or cease?
However, since the waves are not distinct from the moist nature,
the waves likewise have no arising or ceasing.
Therefore, the ancients said:
"The entire earth is a monk’s pair of true eyes;
the entire earth is a monastery."
All of these are the places where those who have realized the principle establish their dwelling and sustain their lives.
Once the true mind is attained,
the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence are simultaneously extinguished.
The mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all the true mind;
apart from this true mind, there is no other place upon which to rely.
Since the delusive causes of the three realms do not exist, [there is nothing else].
There will certainly be no delusive fruits of the six destinies.
Since delusive fruits do not exist, what could they possibly rely upon?
There will certainly be neither "this" nor "that."
Since there is neither "self" nor "other," what can be acceptable and what unacceptable?
Thus, the worlds of the ten directions are but the single true mind;
one experiences them with one's whole being, having no separate basis upon which to rely.
Furthermore, within the gateway of manifesting [births], one is able to take birth according to one's will without obstruction.
Thus, the *Chuan deng lu* records that Minister Wen Cao asked Guifeng:
When a person who has realized the principle reaches the end of their single lifetime, upon what can they rely? Guifeng said:
"All sentient beings are without exception endowed with the spirit-like, luminous, and awakened nature, which is no different from that of the Buddha."
If one can awaken to this nature, it is the Dharmakāya.
Being fundamentally unborn from the beginning, how could there be any dependence or support?
It is spiritually luminous and unclouded, clearly and constantly aware.
It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
it takes emptiness and stillness as its very essence.
Do not mistake it for the physical body.
Take luminous awareness as your own mind;
do not identify with deluded thoughts.
If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all.
Then, at the time of death, one will naturally not be bound by karma;
although there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one’s destination is free,
and one may take up residence as one wishes among the heavens or the human realm.
This is precisely that which was previously referred to as the "True Mind" (zhēn xīn) and that which follows after the body;
the direct exposition of the True Mind concludes here.
